What federal government assistance has been given to municipalities in Canada towards the cost of building up civil defence against air raids, in the form of (a) cash contributions; (b) equipment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The federal government has, since the re-activation of the civil defence organization in 1948, supplied a great deal of assistance to provincial and municipal civil defence organizations in the form of (a) training programs for key civil defence personnel; (b) consultation and help in organizing for civil defence on a local level; and (c) equipment. At the beginning of the current fiscal year, the federal government extended this aid to include financial assistance to support approved provincial and local civil defence projects on a matching basis with the provinces. For this purpose the sum of $1,400,000 is included in the estimates for the current fiscal year. In accordance with long established practice, the federal government does not, of course, deal directly with the municipalities, but with the provinces, and one of the requirements of the grant-in-aid program is that any municipal project receiving federal financial aid must be matched by provincial funds in an amount equal to the federal contribution. Any municipal civil defence project recommended by the province and approved by the federal authorities can qualify for financial aid, either in part or wholly, on the basis of equal contributions from provincial and federal governments. Up to the present time, every project submitted by a provincial civil defence authority under the grant-in-aid program has received
Questions
federal approval, with the exception of one project which is currently under consideration.
(a)	1,776 provincial and municipal civil defence workers-the great majority of whom are municipal-have to date been trained entirely at federal expense in federally sponsored and financed training courses.
(b)	The services of federal consultants in the various branches of civil defence activity are at all times available to assist municipal civil defence authorities, although it is ordinarily expected that requests for such help be channelled through the appropriate civil defence authorities.
(c)	Civil defence equipment and supplies distributed by the federal civil defence authorities to the provinces for use by provincial and municipal civil defence organizations total to date approximately $999,000 in value. This includes a wide variety of training equipment and some operational equipment. The great bulk of it is intended for use in municipal civil defence programs. Included in the above-mentioned total are such items as:
(1) air raid sirens for installation in municipal target areas, $112,000; (2) respirators, $444,000; (3) steel helmets, $133,000;	(4)
coveralls, $65,000; (5) triangular bandages, $42,000.
(d)	Under the grant-in-aid program, three provinces-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia-have to date submitted 15 projects totalling in amount $318,274. These totals include both provincial and municipal civil defence projects. Federal approval has been given to all but one of these projects, and the total federal financial commitment in respect of these projects amounts to $159,137. The project which has not yet been approved is currently under consideration.
Federal financial assistance is available for the support of provincial and municipal civil defence undertakings in the other provinces on the same basis as in the three above-mentioned: and it is anticipated that other provinces will shortly be taking advantage of this arrangement.

This subject is one which has been under consideration for some considerable time, and the very fact that it has is a reason why we should now be perfectly sure where we are headed in dealing with this most important question. It was fully under discussion at the time that the dominion and provincial governments met in 1945. It will be remembered by those who attended that conference that the dominion government put forward certain health proposals, but they proposed a special tax for those measures and so far we have not yet had any clear statement of the alternative. I can remember what I said on behalf of the province of Ontario as recorded in the record of the discussions at page 236. I said:
The dominion government proposes that the provinces finance their share of the cost of health insurance by "a registration fee to be paid by or on behalf of every person who has attained his sixteenth birthday and whose normal place of residence is in the province or area where benefits are provided ..." But anyone who has had experience with the collection of a poll tax will understand the difficulty of collecting a registration fee which is not related to earning capacity, or whether the registrant is employed, an old age pensioner, or a student without personal earning power.
The dominion minister of health and welfare, as well as certain dominion officials, have also stated that the dominion government intends to finance its share of the cost of health insurance or old age pensions by a social security tax levied on all incomes, without exemption. While the amount to be levied in this way was not definitely stated, nor was this special tax in fact mentioned in the printed "Proposals", the figure which has been mentioned in discussion is 5 per cent. This would be in addition to present income taxes and the registration fee or poll tax to be levied by the provinces. This would mean that if the provinces relinquished their personal income and corporation taxes and succession duties, the tax field left to them would be further crowded and confused by the dominion government introducing its special income levy.
That point was made at that time, and ever since has been before the members who attended that conference. Therefore I would recall this to those who now say, "Let us go ahead with the 1945 proposals". Before we go ahead with the 1945 proposals, we must know how they will operate. We must know how they are to be financed and we must know whether the provinces and the municipalities are able to carry out their share. At the moment that information is simply not available.
So far as the subject of health insurance is concerned, there were statements over and over again that there was agreement in principle and that the necessary course was to find out the way that it was to be done. The whole problem is one which necessarily brings

The Address-Mr. Drew the municipalities, hospital boards and provincial governments into the question. I should like to read the closing paragraphs of a very thoughtful and thought-provoking article in the October issue of the McGill Medical Journal by Dr. R. P. Vivian, Strath-cona professor and chairman of the department of health and social medicine at McGill university. After examining this whole question of the problem of the costs of medical care and the various ways in which this service can be assured to everyone, Dr. Vivian closes his article with these words:
There can be no real solution to the complex problem of costs of medical care until the matter is approached jointly by representatives with authority from the professions, hospital boards and governments. Compulsory health insurance does not provide the solution to the matters represented here. The amount of money required would raise the present level of taxes significantly with no assurance of adequate control or acceptable service. It is doubted if the public would appreciate another increase in the tax load.
It would seem that the responsibility for initiating a full exploration of the problem lies with the dominion government. To achieve an improvement in the method of meeting costs of medical care it will require the full co-operation of the professions and the hospitals and the general public. It is hoped that this may occur in the reasonably near future so that the problem may be simplified if not solved.
Mr. Speaker, that statement by an eminent doctor, whose services have been sought by the governments of a number of other countries to consider this very subject, puts its finger right on the problem before us, as do the medical reports which were tabled in the house by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Those reports make it perfectly clear that it is not yet possible for any arbitrary plan to be laid down and that it would, in fact, set back the whole course of improved medical service in this country if a rigid pattern were established by legislation before there was agreement about how provincial authorities, municipal councils, boards of health and other official organizations would play their part in carrying it into effect.
I can understand the sense of urgency in the minds of those who call for action of some kind no matter what the constitutional provisions may be. I can understand the sense of urgency with which that demand is made by those who have themselves felt the full impact of the present cost of treatment of this kind. I think every hon. member in this house shares the desire to provide a system which will assure every Canadian af the very highest level of diagnostic, preventative, medical and surgical treatment, as

well as hospital and other curative treatment that may go with it.
Mr. Speaker, let us not, however, disregard the position of the provinces. Let us not for a moment disregard the fact that it would be impossible to carry this plan out until there is an over-all agreement on the financial position of the provinces. One province as yet has not signed an agreement in regard to taxation. That province has a perfect right to take the position it has taken. The province of Quebec, in its judgment, has decided that it will not sign the agreement that has been offered. How can any plan be put forward while that situation exists? But, Mr. Speaker, I hope no hon. member will suggest that it is the province of Quebec which is preventing this being carried out. No other province can carry it out under the agreement which now exists. It is not the province of Quebec that is holding this up in any way, and do not let anyone suggest it.
The provinces that have signed have made agreements which provide them with certain financial resources to meet present demands. At the time Ontario recently signed an agreement, the prime minister of Ontario made it perfectly clear that this was only a stopgap arrangement and that it did not meet their present requirements. The premier of Nova Scotia has made the same statement, and so have the premiers of other provinces.
It is perfectly clear, therefore, that the provinces are not in a position to carry out their part in any plan of this kind which might be imposed upon them by legislation. Also it is perfectly clear, and it was made abundantly clear by the mayors who met here in Ottawa last week, that the municipalities cannot carry any added burden. In fact they find it difficult to carry their present burdens without some arrangements being made so they will have still further resources. It is the municipalities that must accept the -major share of responsibility for administration in any plan of this kind. You cannot ask them to accept that responsibility under existing arrangements.
It was for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that we introduced the amendment we did, expressing our regret that the government has failed-
(d) To conduct Inquiries in consultation with the provincial governments, so that necessary information may be available for the dominion and provincial governments to consider jointly a national health insurance program.
For the very reasons I have pointed out- the statements that have been made in reports of the provincial governments, the statements that have been made by the dominion government itself at the time these subjects were

Before the vote on the subamendment is taken I too wish to say a few words regarding health insurance. However, I have one or two other things which I first wish to put before the house.
I noticed that when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was speaking in the house the other day, particularly in reply to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), he laid great stress on the progress which has been made in Canada during the last number of years. He pointed out that the prosperity of Canada had reached an all-time height; that the national product of this country had reached something like $22 billion; but at the same time, and this was somewhat significant, 10
per cent of our national product had to go for defence. Let me state immediately that Social Credit policy has never been niggardly in respect to the money which was required for national defence. If you go back even to 1935, when we first came into this house,
I believe the record will show that we have been among those who were always advocating that there was nothing too good for our servicemen, particularly those men who were facing the enemy over in Korea or anywhere else. We believed that they should have the best of equipment, the best of clothing and the best of everything it was possible to give them.
We join with others in that regard; and we want to indicate also that we are proud of the fact that Canada has prospered as it has. We must not be confused, however; and this is the point that was raised by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) the other day, when he stated that this prosperity was in great part the result of the efforts of the federal government. Of course I dealt with that once before in this house, and I do not intend to reiterate what I said on that occasion. I was impressed with a magazine which I received yesterday, and which is published in Alberta. It is entitled Within our Borders. I should like to give a quotation from the issue of December 1, 1952, as an indication of the progress that has been made through other efforts than those of the federal government. The heading on this article is "Alberta industrial employment doubles in 13 years". It reads:
Alberta's manufacturing industry is estimated to have a gross value of production of $510 million this year. This compares to a gross production value of $87 million in 1939.
You will note that it was in the fall of 1935 that the Social Credit government took over the reins in Alberta. You will notice also the tremendous results since then.
Between 1939 and 1952, employment in Alberta's manufacturing industry has increased from 13,000 to 29,000 while the number of establishments has grown from 1,000 to 1,900. More than 11 per cent of Alberta's labour force is employed in the manufacturing industry while 25 per cent are employed in other industries. Agriculture absorbs 38 per cent of the working force and other primary industries 9 per cent.
New investment in Alberta's manufacturing industries has soared since 1947. In this year, new investment amounted to $10,700,000; in 1950, $16 million; in 1951, $24,400,000 and 1952 will see an estimated $77,400,000 invested in industry. Investment in manufacturing has increased 623 per cent from 1947 to 1952 or 390 per cent when allowances are made to offset inflationary values. Profits of Alberta companies increased slightly more than 100 per cent between 1946 and 1950.
That will give hon. members some indication of the progress that can be made in this country under proper provincial supervision.

The Address-Mr. Johnston The big trouble is that at the same time there has been an increase in municipal debt. Let me give you an example. The mayor of Calgary, one of those municipalities that has gone head over heels in debt, was the Liberal candidate in the last federal election. There you have a good example of the policy of Liberal administration. If you want to correct these evils, and correct them quickly, the only answer is to get rid of those Liberals and get a Social Credit regime. Then you will find, as I have indicated, that you will have prosperity.
A moment ago I mentioned that the Prime Minister had indicated that 10 per cent of our national product had to go for defence. In other words, the budget amounted to something over $4 billion and about half of that goes to national defence. This gives us the basis for the belief that it is the national defence spending which is maintaining prosperity in Canada today. It gives a stimulus to business which would not otherwise be there. It is a sad state of affairs, Mr. Speaker, when the prosperity of our country must be dependent upon preparation for war. If you removed that factor from our economy today you would find we would be facing another depression.
One of the signs which indicate that times are not as good as they might be, when you consider our national product is as high as it is-and this was indicated the other day by the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch)-is the fact that so many people in Canada are now forced to buy on credit. It i:s quite evident that if the people of this country had sufficient purchasing power they would not be using their credit to buy these things which are necessary. You only have to pick up a newspaper to see that refrigerators and washing machines are advertised at greatly reduced prices. If you go to a store to buy a washing machine they will give you $75 or $100 for your old machine without even looking at it. They are trying to force people who have not the money to buy these things into credit buying. Conditions would be a great deal worse if it were not for the fact that we are spending $2 billion and more each year for war production, and this money is spread out among the people so they have that amount available as purchasing power to buy consumer goods. Otherwise we would be in a very poor position.
It is tragic when one realizes that we have to depend on this type of an economy in order to maintain any sign of prosperity. This morning I was in the railway committee room and heard Mr. Dymond speak at the meeting of the advisory council on labour. He made some outstanding statements about the subject I was discussing. Mr. Dymond 
told us, and I took a note of it, that defence is the underlying support of our economy. It struck me as rather important, because that was the thing I intended to deal with this afternoon. This statement was made by one of the government officials in the Department of Labour, that the underlying support of our economy is our defence effort.
What would happen if our war effort were to fold up? What would happen if peace were declared in this world? I am not suggesting for a moment that everyone would not be very happy to have that happen, but what would be the disastrous results to our economy? Mr. Dymond went on to point out that one of the reasons for fuller employment was that the war industries had now reached the point where they were going into quantity production. Even despite that fact, in the figures which were tabled at that meeting this morning it was pointed out that although we have what is generally called a period of high employment, nevertheless there are over 100,000 employable unemployed who cannot find jobs. That is the situation in a period of our peak prosperity.
Those are some of the warnings, Mr. Speaker, which we must take into consideration. There are, as well, other warnings to show that in our economy all is not quite as well as it could be. The other day I was looking through some of the clippings I had in my desk, and I found one from the Calgary Herald of Thursday, October 9, 1952. It is entitled "Production up During July". It is a reprint from Ottawa, Canadian Press, and reads as follows:
The pace of production and business quickened during July, spurred by higher wholesale and retail sales and by heavier output of some metals, electric power, newsprint and automobiles.
As a result, the industrial production index, based on 1935-39 equals 100, increased to 210-8 in July over 208-0 a year ago, the bureau of statistics reported Tuesday. However, for the first seven months this year, production was down about 1-6 per cent from output in the same period in 1951.
The pace of the decline was cut from 2-8 per cent in the first quarter to 9-7 per cent in the second. A drop in manufacturing was the main cause of the slip.
During July, however, gold production increased to 375,000 fine ounces from 344,000 in July, last year; steel climbed to 293,000 tons from 275,000; newsprint, 486,000 tons from 452,000.
The point I should like you to note, Mr. Speaker, is this. Had it not been for the increase in the production of gold, steel and newsprint, that index would have fallen to a greater extent than it did; and the place where the greatest downward trend was shown was in the manufacturing industry. That fact shows quite clearly that our manufacturing industries are not in what one would call a healthy condition; and when

you find that we have something like
100,000	employable unemployed, then the situation needs some looking into.
In this house on many occasions we have heard from members who have indicated a falling off in the production of industries within their constituencies. The one who comes to my mind at the moment is the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) who this year was talking about the way the production of the woollen mills in his constituency had fallen off. These are some of the things we must keep in mind. There are as well other indications that we must watch if we are to have a prosperous Canada. Agriculture is one industry which is in need of some attention. In Canada agriculture has been the basic industry ever since the country first came into existence.

Today we find that those engaged in agriculture are becoming greatly concerned as to how they are going to be able to market their products and yet be able to show a decent profit. It is true that last year the agricultural industry had a fairly good crop but it was of poor grade. Low grades and damp grain made marketing difficult. The wheat board did an excellent job in that respect. This year-that is 1952 -we have had another good crop, but we have also had difficulties in marketing it. Some of the farmers are finding themselves in need of cash because the delivery quotas are so- low.
Agriculture is one industry which must have the greatest amount of attention paid to it lest it too begin to slip back as it did during the hungry thirties. The farmers are conscious of this fact. When they find that the support price of hogs will drop from 26 cents to 23 cents, it causes them a great deal of concern. When they find that their markets for beef have been lost, that fact also gives them a great deal of concern. It is true that the foot-and-mouth disease had something to do with that situation. However, that embargo will be lifted on March 1 and it is to be hoped there will be some relief in that regard. Nevertheless we will still find difficulty in marketing our beef products.
The farmer also finds that he is suffering a loss on the sale of eggs. The same thing is true with regard to dairy products. We cannot have a healthy agricultural industry if we are going to allow prices to drop to the point where farmers cannot make a profit on the things they produce. Particularly is
The Address-Mr. Johnston that true, Mr. Speaker, when we understand that the things which the farmers have to buy are continually rising in price. Even the interest rates are going up on the money which they must borrow in order to carry on their seasonal operations. The price of farm machinery is soaring ever upward. The industries which produce the secondary goods are in such a position that they can control their production in order to maintain prices. But as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) pointed out the other day, what position would this country be in and what position would the world be in if the farmers throughout the nations decided to curtail production in order to maintain prices?
There is throughout Canada a good deal of concern over this problem. Some of the leading papers are taking note of it. The other day I cut out an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, December
4.	It is an editorial which is headed "The Farmers' Case" and it reads as follows:
Forecasts read at the dominion-provincial agricultural conference in Ottawa indicated that the Canadian farmer faces the 1933 prospect of reduced returns for his products with an increase in the cost of services and supplies he has to buy.
This should extinguish for good the suggestion that all farmers are making easy fortunes, although it may be true that the prairie wheat growers, with a record crop and solid prices, have an unusual degree of prosperity.
Delegates who heard the forecasts prepared by government economists make it plain they considered them over-optimistic. The root of the problem they face is found in uncertainty about markets, the United States' embargoes or quotas on dairy imports, and the United Kingdom inability to maintain her traditional purchases of such items as Canadian cheese being two important factors.
In this situation the farmer must look to the dominion government, the central authority in a position to assist in negotiating better trade arrangements and fighting currency difficulties which hamper exports of surpluses.
The farmer with surpluses piling on his farm at a time when millions need more food will feel betrayed if Ottawa fails in the vigorous and effective action they have the right to expect.
When you have a forecast of lower agricultural prices and loss of markets coming from government authorities, Mr. Speaker, it is even more significant that it otherwise would be. In the Ottawa Journal of Monday, December 1, while the dominion-provincial conference was sitting here in Ottawa, there appeared an article headed "Farm Incomes Likely Down Next Year. Federal-Provincial Conference Looks to '53 Program", which reads in part as follows:
Dominion government economists today told the dominion-provincial agricultural conference that farm incomes probably will be somewhat lower in 1953 although the demand for food products will continue high.

The Address-Mr. Johnston
Then Mr. C. V. Parker director of the agricultural division, dominion bureau of statistics, said:
Present prospects gave little indication of a major change in 1953 from the generally prosperous conditions of 1952 in the domestic field.
Export prospects were more uncertain. Due largely to exchange difficulties, sales to some overseas countries were not likely to be maintained at the high levels of 1952.
The exchange difficulties are something for which the federal government is directly responsible. Then Mr. Parker goes on in this way:
Farm net income in 1953 also was expected to be somewhat lower, being calculated by adding income in kind to cash income, deducting farm expenses and depreciation, and adding or subtracting the value of changes in physical inventories of livestock and grains held on farms at the end of the year.
There appeared little prospect of any significant change in total farm operating expenses in 1953, while taxes and interest rates might average higher.
The indication is clear that unless we have some change in the agricultural policy of this country we will be heading for difficulty, bearing in mind always that the greatest factor bolstering our so-called present prosperity is our defence effort. Each one of us hopes, of course, that the defence effort soon will not be needed. But in what condition will our economy be when that comes about?
The government has some responsibility in the matter. It is about to negotiate a new international wheat agreement. The farm unions in the three prairie provinces are asking that a change be made in the price. In some instances they are asking a ceiling of $2.35 with a floor of $1.85. Some organizations in the United States are asking for a price of $2.50. I am not going to suggest what the price should be, but I will say without hesitation that the price set in the international wheat agreement should be considerably higher than it is today. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will be the one responsible for negotiating the agreement. He has said on other occasions that he will be a little tough to deal with; I hope that is true. He is a tough trader, and it is hoped that when the government negotiates the new agreement there will be a considerable increase in price, both in the ceiling and in the floor.
One factor which has been of great benefit to agriculture in the last few years is the fact that we have had a wheat board. But the wheat board is being attacked from every angle. I am sure I speak for the farmers of western Canada when I say that they do not want to do. away with the board. They want to have orderly marketing of the products

they have to offer. We know only too well, through past experience, that the farmers of western Canada particularly have had to sell their grain when prices were at the lowest. That was entirely due to the fact that they were at the mercy of the grain, exchange. All the notes the farmer had given during the year to finance his operations became due immediately after threshing. That was usually the period when prices were low. The grain exchange was able to buy that grain at greatly reduced prices, and made a handsome profit on it. So those people who are lamenting over their loss of revenue because the grain exchange has, to a great extent, been put out of operation, are doing everything within their power to see that the grain exchange comes back into force, and that the wheat board is done away with.
I was interested the other day in reading an article in the Manitoba Co-operator which, it seemed to me, summed up the situation pretty well. Under the heading "Averages", it states:
Stanley Jones, president of the Winnipeg grain exchange, says that the final wheat board payment averaging about 25 cents a bushel on deliveries from the 1951 crop was below the market average. That payment brought the price of wheat to $1.83% basis No. 1 Northern at the terminal.
Mr. Jones had the same remark to make about wheat board payment on barley.
The vice-president of the grain exchange said the same thing about the wheat board payment on oats.
The monotony of this performance might be relieved if a little variety was interjected therein. A well-trained parrot could do the job that is being done equally as well.
Mr. Jones never stops to explain that the average prices he quotes do not take into account storage charges, costs of conditioning tough and damp grain, interest on borrowed money and other expenses.
He does not calculate deliveries on prices prevalent during heavy delivery periods, thus presenting a true picture.
All his efforts are directed to discrediting the wheat board which, as every farmer knows, made a real achievement in marketing the badly damaged 1951 crop.
A comparison might be made with the performance of the open market when it was operating freely in the 1930's. In the six years from 1930 to 1935 inclusive the average price of wheat at the terminal under an unrestricted open market was 69 cents a bushel.
In 1932 Alberta farmers marketed a big crop of good quality and obtained therefrom the average price of 32 cents a bushel. They lost money on every bushel they produced.
I think that article sums up the situation so far as the grain exchange is concerned. I need not add anything further. But let no one think that the farmers of western Canada want to do away with the wheat board.
I should like to say a few words about old age pensions, and pensions for incurables. These are classes of people who require our

attention. There can be no doubt in my mind that almost every member in the house -and I use the word "almost" advisedly- would be in favour of increasing old age pensions, if it were put to an open and free vote in the house. I think the basis for determining an increased pension should not necessarily be, "Have we the money to increase the pension?" but rather, "Can we produce it? Have we the goods and services to provide increased pensions, without interfering in any way with the prosperity and progress of the country?"
I am sure the answer is that we can well afford to increase pensions. When we consider that our national product is in the neighbourhood of $22 billion, when we sit here and listen to the Prime Minister speak about the prosperity of Canada, and when we listen to hon. members speak about the great future of Canada, we should not hesitate to give increased pensions to those in need. Not only have we the actual production, but we have a great potential production.
This past season we had the largest crop of the very finest wheat in the history of Canada. Who will dare say that under those circumstances we cannot give our old age pensioners another loaf of bread? Who will dare say that with proper marketing conditions and proper inducements to agriculture we cannot give our old age pensioners or our incurables another pound of bacon, another dozen of eggs or another pound of butter? Surely there is no one in his right senses who will say that we cannot afford to raise old age pensions. Yet the lamentable fact is that the pensions are not being raised.
I know it will be said they were raised to $40 a month without the means test, which is something worth while, but it must be understood that today people cannot live on $40 a month any better than during the period of the depression they could live on $20 a month. You will therefore see the need of some further increases.
I received a letter from an old age pensioners' association which I think I should place on Hansard. It is from the Alberta old age pensioners' society, Calgary branch, and is addressed to me as the member of parliament for the constituency of Bow River, and I want to recognize this letter. This letter reads:
Dear Mr. Johnston:
May we draw your kind attention to the following points and requests?
In 1940 when this branch was first formed our older citizens of seventy were endeavouring to "exist" on twenty dollars basic pension monthly. Mr. Speaker, this debate has become so dead that I do not suppose I can make it any more so. In any event, I should like to speak for about ten minutes on one specific subject, the level of taxation in Canada. I am going to contend today, as I have over the past year, that federal taxes are now at the danger point. I believe that the national interest requires a sharp reduction, and I should like to make such a proposal to parliament at this time.
As hon. members know, our expenditures in 1952 are going to exceed $4,500 million, which is about ten times what they were in 1939. I would remind hon. members that even in the crucial years of world war II, in 1940, 1941, 1942 and 1943, when we were fighting for our very life as a nation, our budgets did not exceed the figure of the current budget. On only one occasion since confederation have federal taxes been so high. Most Canadians are paying more money out in taxes today, than for food. To my mind that is a dangerous situation.
It is small wonder that a great many citizens are becoming increasingly restive under the high level of taxation. Like other Canadians I am not going to take exception to taxes raised, first, for essential government expenditures; second, for social welfare programs which are provided by this parliament, or, third, for national defence. But like most Canadians I am becoming thoroughly fed up with the government policy of overtaxation, on the one hand, and its failure to eliminate waste and extravagance, on the other.
During the debate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) told us that in his opinion there had not been much overtaxation. What are the facts? The first fiscal year under the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott! commenced on April 1, 1947. The period from that date to October 31 of this year represents 2,131 days. During that time the Liberal government has taken from the pockets of the Canadian taxpayer $2,150 million more than they have been able to spend. In other words, since the present Minister of Finance took office there has been overtaxation each and every day, including Sundays and holidays, of more than $1 million. Yet the Prime Minister blandly tells us that in his opinion there has not been overtaxation. I suggest that the figures speak for themselves.
It is rather interesting to note that during the same period United States investments


in Canada in our iron ore, our oil, our aluminum and other fields have been roughly $2,000 million. I think it is reasonable to suggest that if the Canadian tax rate had not been so harsh, Canadians might have financed a greater share of our post-war investment [DOT] program.
The huge surpluses we have had in recent years have not been effected by economy; rather they have been accomplished despite a substantial amount of extravagance in government spending. Several years ago the Minister of Finance, his parliamentary assistant at that time, and others gave us the assurance that non-defence expenditures were going to be curtailed and rigidly restricted. As a matter of fact I think some minister said some would be deferred in the interests of the defence effort. Apparently that promise has been forgotten, because Canada's non-defence expenditures this year are almost triple what they were at the end of the war. Spending is going on unabated, and the expenditures of almost every non-defence department are up substantially.
I have here a summary of departmental expenditures for the first seven months of the current fiscal year compared with the same period in 1951. From April 1 to October 31 of this year every single department of government but one has had substantially increased expenditures. The only one which has not is the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Of course the reason for that apparent exception is that there was a census last year conducted by the bureau of statistics, and there is no expenditure for a census this year. In the seven months period I have mentioned, nondefence expenditures have gone up, compared with the same seven months last year, by $231 million. If there is any evidence of economy there I wish someone would tell me where it is.
I am going to say that the so-called economy drive announced by the minister several years ago is a complete failure. I think it was a political farce from the beginning. The Minister of Finance has discounted and disparaged suggestions that have been made for economies. He does not seem to be very much interested in the subject. I can tell him and parliament that the people of the country generally are bewildered and concerned over the attitude the Minister of Finance is taking in this regard. Since I came here I have tried to figure out why the government does not seem to be particularly interested in savings. Some hon. members may laugh, but I think one of the reasons is that there are not enough businessmen here in Ottawa.

Parliament is running a $4| billion business, the biggest business anywhere in the nation, yet we are following practices and methods that would cause any corporation to go bankrupt if it were to do likewise. Take, for example, the fantastic duplication of effort right in this very building. We have two post offices, two or three police forces, two messenger staffs, two journals branches, two stenographic staffs, two treasury offices and so on all down the line. What business corporation in Canada would not remedy such a situation, particularly if the duplication were pointed out to it?
The taxpayer of Canada is the man who today is being taxed for waste of that kind. I think the composition of the cabinet is rather interesting. I looked through the Canadian Parliamentary Guide the other day and I find that of the twenty cabinet members, fourteen are lawyers, three are engineers, one is classed as a farmer, one is a doctor and one is a businessman. I think the professions represented are all excellent, but I cannot help wondering whether, if we had a few more businessmen and perhaps a coal miner and a few farmers thrown in here and there, we would not start to get the kind of government which would be interested in economy in order to bring down the tax rate. I think such a reform should be considered by the Prime Minister the next time he shuffles the membership of his cabinet.
I say that high taxes are lowering our standard of living and discouraging initiative generally. The amazing feature of the present situation is that the Minister of Finance quite nonchalantly and quite freely admits that taxes are too high. He made a series of tours during the past summer during which he spoke on taxation. I am only going to quote a sentence from one speech he made. On that occasion he was speaking in London, and the Canadian Press quotes him as follows:
I agree with almost everybody that tax rates are uncomfortably high and that we ought to follow tax policies which will lead towards lower rates.
That statement is very clear. The minister acknowledges that taxes are too high; yet, despite repeated representations by individuals and business concerns, despite unprecedented surpluses, the minister has done nothing so far to reduce taxation. Why? We can only assume because he is waiting for an election year. The Minister of Finance has told Canadians up and down the country that they can expect tax relief if and when they increase production and efficiency. I want to tell the minister and this parliament that high taxes in Canada today are doing more
The Address-Mr. Thatcher than any other single thing to lower production and efficiency. Because of high taxes there is a tendency in Canada today for individuals and corporations to become tax conscious rather than efficiency conscious.
I know of married women working at parttime employment who have quit their jobs when their income reached a certain point, because they did not want to be in a higher income tax category. There are many working people who are not interested in overtime work because so much of the additional pay goes to the tax collector. Every hon. member, those from western Canada at least, knows of farmers who have gone out of the production of hogs or livestock or poultry. Why? Because, as they put it, why should they work fourteen hours a day for Mr. Abbott? There are in Canada today business firms, corporations, which seek methods of spending profits on unnecessary advertising, donations, extra equipment or repairs, rather than be bled white by the Department of National Revenue.
I say that today there is growing hesitancy on the part of business firms to expand. If the new project is successful, the Minister of Finance takes most of the profits; but if, on the other hand, the project is a failure then the financial stability of the whole organization is jeopardized.

I should like to suggest several tax cuts to the Minister of Finance for his next budget. In the first place, there should be a 2 per cent cut in the general sales tax. Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to reply in a few words to this ten-minute speech on the subject of taxation, not that I am any

longer connected with the finance department but merely to answer the remarks made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). Many hon. members will remember that most of what he said was incorporated in his now famous taxation speech of a year ago.
I would like particularly to comment on the figures he gave when speaking about the federal budget, and to show exactly where costs were increased. He pointed out, initially, that the federal budget today is roughly ten times what it was in 1939. However the whole pattern of the federal budget has changed very much since then. Out of this $44 billion budget, approximately half goes for defence spending as a result of Korea and communist aggression around the world. He did point out in this speech that he was not criticizing the defence spending, necessary as it is, so we can get on from this item.
The next great expenditure-very briefly and without breaking it down into departments-is $1 billion for federal social security measures under four main categories: old age pensions; family allowances; veterans' pensions and allowances; and the government's contribution to unemployment insurance. This $1 billion is not government spending in the sense that economists refer to government spending. The government does not spend this money by hiring people or buying material. This is money taken out of the taxation stream and paid as cash to various groups in Canada, for instance to the aged, as far as old age pensions are concerned, and as family allowances to the mothers of Canada. In this field I have never heard his group suggest that we should economize by cutting down spending on old age pensions. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will agree with that. As far as the cost of family allowances is concerned, again if we are going to save taxes there we would have to cut back cn family allowances. The hon. member for Moose Jaw may have his own opinions but I know the opinion of his party is that we should not economize in that way. Similar arguments prevail as far as unemployment insurance is concerned and as far as veterans' pensions and allowances are concerned. The only way to reduce the taxes necessary to pay for these measures is to reduce these benefits and pensions.
That $1 billion is entirely transfer payments. It is not spending by the government. It is taken in taxes from those who have done very well in this country, from those who are in the high income brackets. Taxation takes 52 per cent of the profits from every

successful business corporation in this country as a share for all of Canada in that prosperity, and that pattern has been approved by this parliament. These social security payments were initiated by the Liberal party and approved by this house. Never on the hustings, other than in the city of Moose Jaw, have I heard criticism of those payments, by the party to which he belongs, so taxes can not be cut on this billion dollars.
That takes care of $2J billion for defence and $1 billion for social security, expenditures of which his party has no criticism. The next item is caused by the fact that we did fight a war to save our freedom, the most expensive war in all history. We financed that war, because of the courageous financial action taken by Mr. Ilsley, better than any other country in the world as far as paying a greater percentage of the cost of the war out of current taxation is concerned. Nevertheless we did have to borrow as well. This time we did not borrow abroad. We did not borrow as we did in the first war, under Conservative management, at 5| per cent income tax free. We borrowed from the Canadian people at 3 per cent, subject to income tax. These war loans are an obligation to the Canadian people and each year our estimates show-last year speaking from memory it was $425 million-an item to meet interest payments on our national debt. Nine-tenths of the national debt today was incurred as a consequence of the war.
When my hon. friend says we have racked up surpluses, of course we have. That policy was announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in 1945 in his famous white paper on post-war policy -that in good years we would have surpluses and reduce debt, the policy followed by all good businesses. That is the only way we can ever reduce that large fixed charge for interest payments on our national debt. The $425 million in our budget each year is again not being spent by the Canadian government to employ men or buy materials. It is a transfer of money raised in taxes as interest payments to those Canadians who loaned us money during the war to prosecute the war.
There are two ways in which we can cut down in our debt. One is what the Social Credit government did in 1935, to repudiate our loans. We will never do that. The only other way we can do it is to reduce the principal of the loan and so save interest payments. We are reducing our national debt each year. It is to the great credit of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. The Address-Mr. Sinclair Abbott) that in his period of office each year has been distinguished by a surplus. He has reduced our national debt by over $2 billion-almost 20 per cent-and no other country in the world can say that.
If my hon. friend suggests that we could have invested this money in Ungava or Kitimat or other places, he does not realize, or he chooses not to realize, that it is principally because we have such a sound financial administration here in Canada that we have attracted money from every part of the world for investment in Canada. The great criticism of Americans who come up here to invest is that in their own country they have this deficit spending. The United States government spend each year more than they raise in taxation, deficits which add to their tax burden.
My hon. friend was careful not to mention another new item in our federal budget-the tax rental agreements now signed by nine out of ten provinces. I spoke on them last summer, after the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) had spoken roundly condemning them, and I expressed the hope at that time that the good judgment of Premier Frost would soon lead him to enter' into such an agreement. I am very happy to say that he has seen the value of these tax rental agreements which help to equalize opportunity in all provinces. These agreements also return to the provinces much more than they were ever able to collect themselves. We are today collecting on behalf of the provinces $300 million in round figures from income taxes, corporation taxes, and succession duties which we pay back to them. We do not spend it. We do not spend it on materials and labour. It is again a straight transfer of cash back to the provinces. The provinces are very heartily in accord with it and why should they not be? The federal government gets all the criticism for high taxes, and passes on the money. They get the money but no criticism. The hon. member's own province, Saskatchewan, was never able to collect one-quarter as much in those fields as they get today from the federal government by renting them to us. All this results in another $300 million to be collected by the Minister of Finance. The hon. member will not want to cut taxes by reducing the payments to his province.
Taking those new fields, defence expenditures and cash transfers to the Canadian people and provinces off the total expenditure of the federal budget, in round figures we are left with about $700 million for all other expenditures-the normal expenditures to provide all the services of government in Canada. That is only about twice the figure

This was a very popular rumour in the shipyards in my own riding during wartime, that if you worked extra hours you were going to lose money. Nobody in Canada, by working extra hours, can lose money. Most of the extra earnings is left to him, that is unless he is one of these very successful business operators who has so greatly expanded his business in the post-war years that he is now in the high income tax brackets. Then, you do pay a larger part in taxes, but some of the extra earnings still remain with even the millionaire.
The hon. member used this phrase-it sort of surprised me to hear a socialist member using it-that business is being bled white in this country and hesitated to expand because of too heavy taxation. Those were his words. What is the story in this country? Never in history has there been such a tremendous business expansion in every part of the country as in the last seven years, with no sign of hesitancy. In past debates my hon. friend has always been quite ready to use personal examples. I would suggest that the sort of expansion he has seen in his own business in the last seven years gives the lie to this statement about business being bled white, and that business hesitates to expand. He has become in these years, instead of a one-man hardware merchant, a tycoon running a chain of stores in Saskatchewan.

Seven years have passed in rapid deterioration in world relations and, shall I say, in the morale of the world; and conditions are far worse than they were in 1945.
I should like to read excerpts from four speeches by men whom I think the house will respect, which excerpts indicate the truth of what I have just said. The executive directors of the international monetary fund in their 1952 annual report stated:

The third serious problem we have to face is the widespread balance of payments disequilibrium affecting many countries. While there is surplus production in many areas and acute needs in others, trade cannot flow because of the lack of needed currency.
Here is another one from "Trade Winds" from Babson's "Washington Forecast", September 22, 1952:
U.S. exports and imports are still dropping. While we still maintain a favourable balance of trade, storm warnings are up around the world. In spite of all our economic aid and overseas procurement, the big bugaboo is the off-shore dollar shortage. Dollars were more plentiful abroad after our post-Korea spending spree. That was followed by a strong foreign market for our products. Now, the dollars are running out. As a result, our exports have dropped an average of almost 10 per cent per month since early spring.

One more from "A World Economic Crisis" in Whaley-Eaton Service, September 6, 1952:
A world economic crisis is in the making, as indicated in the report of the International Monetary Fund to the effect that financial conditions have worsened. There has been a backslide towards a tangle of restrictive money and trade controls. Solutions are yet to be forthcoming. The British are expected to have a major program ready for presentation to the next American president soon after the election. As reported last week, this will probably call for removal of trade barriers to a degree heretofore not contemplated.
To all those who have been giving careful thought to international affairs, who have studied with some understanding causes of world war II and world war I and the cause of the great depression which led to world war II, may I suggest that the statements contained in those comments carry the gravest import. Those quotations indicate strongly that our main problem in the world is a monetary problem. We in this group have been contending in season and out of season ever since we came here in 1936 that our problem is a monetary problem. We must not expect to find a solution in any other direction.
Let us then give the minutest attention to our monetary system. Thus far our pleadings, shall I say, have largely fallen on deaf ears. Members of the Conservative party, members of the C.C.F. party and some Liberals have begun to wonder how in the world it was that the Social Crediters were right on Bretton Woods while they were all wrong, but it has not dawned on them that Social Crediters knew some great fundamental facts about trade and money matters in this world which unfortunately these gentlemen either had not learned or had not learned their significance. Once more I call the attention of the house and the country, and our neighbouring countries if they will listen, to the fact that our problem is a monetary problem especially if war preparation ceases in the world.
Money is a remarkable mechanism. There is nothing mysterious about it. There is nothing sacred about money. Money is created by man to meet man's convenience and to help man solve his problems of production and distribution. Money ought to be the servant of man, but up to the present time in the history of the world money has been the master of man and has caused man some of the most grievous torture that he has experienced on this planet. On the face of the earth there is not one dollar, one pound, one mark, one franc, one lira, yen or ruble that human agencies have not brought into being.
Why do men dread money? Why do they fear the proposal that a government should
The Address-Mr. Blackmore create money, when the constitutions of the United States and Canada specifically give the central government the authority and the responsibility to create money and do not say that they should put that responsibility on the shoulders of bankers? The kings of Great Britain created the nation's money, and the money was the king's money for centuries. In those days the country was happier, considering the progress of economic affairs, than it has ever been since the bankers began to create money.
The result of .the whole thing is that we have had plenty of trouble. What is the reason that men fear money? Everybody in the house and in the country knows that too much money in the economy tends to cause inflation or a rise of prices through having too few goods in relation to the money in circulation. In other words there would be too many dollars chasing too few goods, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) put it so well one time, causing a scarcity of goods and a rise in their price. Too little money in an economy tends to cause deflation or a fall in prices and employment, through having too many goods in relation to the money in circulation or, in other words, too few dollars chasing too many goods.
Certainly it ought to occur to everybody that one of the main things mankind should aim at, in this day and age particularly, is a device whereby the amount of money can be kept in constant relation to the amount of goods so there would be at all times the right amount of money chasing the right amount of goods. It should not be impossible for an age that has created radar, guided missiles, the jet plane, the atom bomb, the hydrogen bomb, that has contemplated flights into space, to create a device which would guarantee that regular relation between money in circulation and goods available for purchase. Why is it that apparently nobody, except Social Crediters, has given any attention to this matter? It strikes me as astounding.
Usually there have been present complicating factors, which is one reason it has been hard to tie down any particular aspect of inflation or deflation. The result of it all has been that monetary science is as yet utterly inadequate and its conclusions bitterly contentious. An example of that is to be found in our own day and generation. An increase in prices in the United States and Canada has been deliberately manipulated by crudely and sordidly selfish men, and now practically all statesmen are endeavouring to show that that increase in prices was the result of too much money, which is a preposterous falsehood.

The Address-Mr. Blackmore In Canada the increase in prices commenced in 1946, as I have pointed out to the house time and again, with the increase of $5 a ton in steel. From there it spread until it affected the whole Canadian price structure and put that structure on the skids. For any person in his right senses to try to blame that rise in prices on too much money is for him to be either fantastically and naively uninformed and unenlightened or deliberately hypocritical, one of the two. I imagine that the period from 1946 to 1951 will go down in history as one of the evidences of the bad results of having too much money in circulation! It is merely a complicating factor which makes it so difficult for men to come to understand the true facts about money. I should like to read one short quotation before I ask to adjourn the debate, because I

think it is better that it should be included in today's Hansard. Sir Basil Blackett had these words to say in 1931:
In view of what we have done with currency and currency with us in the last twenty years, we are all of us fit for the lunatic asylum. If many currency experts go mad, it is the natural result of their coming face to face with the insanity of the monetary system with which man has tortured himself ever since he passed from barter to money.
Twenty-one years have passed since the writing of those words, and they are probably doubly true today. Still the horrible insanity goes on.
